name: Nikhil Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the office for a small architecture practice, nine of us above a bike shop. I do the diary for the partners, book site visits, chase invoices, and keep the drawing files in order, which is harder than it sounds because architects name files like toddlers. I'm still the junior, and I'm still learning the invoicing side, but I've set up AI to draft the meeting notes and sort the inbox every morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: So AI is already part of your day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day, yeah. I record the Monday meeting, the AI writes the minutes, and I fix the bits it gets wrong, like when it thought 'soffit' was a person. It saves me maybe an hour a day, and I spend that hour learning the invoicing I'm still slow at. My boss thinks I'm a wizard, which is funny because I left school at eighteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say, told you so, it's a good tool, not a god. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts. Online I'd post that the real story was always who gets the time it saves, the worker or the boss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I'm fine. My job stays, the hour a day I save stays mine, and I keep being the person who knows the tools. Rent's the only thing that bites, it went up again in September.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now, mostly. I'd keep building little automations for the office, and I'd ask for a pay rise in the spring review, because I'm doing more than when I started. I'd keep putting money aside, we've got about four months saved between us, Lena and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty relaxed. A bit bored, maybe, because I like it when things move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent bites. How much room is there, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not loads. Lena's a nurse and works nights, so with both wages we're fine, but one bad month, like the boiler going, eats the savings. That's about the only thing I'd lie awake over in this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who keeps the time AI saves at your office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I keep the time AI saves, because nobody else at the office knows how long the minutes used to take. In the long run I think the partners would notice and pile more on me. That's why I'd want a union, even in a tiny office.

say: I'd say AI is a **good tool**, not a god, and keep sharing shortcuts.
Online I'd argue the real question is who keeps the **time it saves**.
think: My job is **safe**, and I stay the one who knows the tools.
The only thing that bites is **rent**, which rose again in September.
do: Keep building **small automations** for the office diary and inbox.
Ask for a **pay rise** at the spring review for the extra work.
Keep adding to the **four months** of savings Lena and I share.
feel: **Relaxed**, maybe a little **bored**, because he likes change.
S0.quote: Right now I keep the time AI saves, because nobody else at the office knows how long the minutes used to take.
fieldNote: Daily AI user who sees himself as the office's **tool expert** despite being junior.
Money pressure is real but limited: **rent rises** and one-off shocks.
Progressive lens: he frames saved time as a **fairness** question between staff and bosses.

steps.text: Build automations for the partners' diary and inbox
Ask for a pay rise at the spring review
Add to the four months of shared savings each payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for unions and rules, because the change is real and people need a say. At work I'd tell the partners we should use it to take on more projects, not to cut people. I'd be the one running the lunch-and-learn sessions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm the guy automating himself. Booking, invoicing, filing, minutes, that's the list on your card, and I've already done half of it with AI. I think the practice keeps me if I'm the one running the systems, and drops me if I'm just doing the tasks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to become the practice's systems person, officially, with that in my job title. I'd do an online course in IT support in the evenings, so I've got something on paper, because right now I've only got school. And I'd join the union for office staff, even though nobody else at work is in one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a fizzy way. Like the floor's moving but I've got good shoes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're below average at the invoicing side. Does that worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. If AI does invoicing perfectly, then my weak spot vanishes, which is funny. But it also means the thing I'm still learning isn't worth learning, so I'd stop trying to get good at it and spend that time on the systems side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agnes, our receptionist, who's been there since before the practice moved. She hates computers, she prints her emails. I'd try to help her, but honestly if the practice has to choose between us, it picks me, and that doesn't feel great.

say: I'd say this is when **unions and rules** matter, because the change is real.
I'd tell the partners to use AI to win **more projects**, not cut people.
think: I've already **automated half** of the tasks on this list myself.
The practice keeps me only if I **run the systems**, not just do tasks.
do: Ask for an official **systems role** in my job title.
Take an evening **IT support course** to get a qualification on paper.
Join the **office staff union**, even as the only member at work.
feel: **Uneasy** but **fizzy**, like the floor's moving and he's in good shoes.
S1.quote: I think the practice keeps me if I'm the one running the systems, and drops me if I'm just doing the tasks.
fieldNote: He sees clearly that his own tasks are **on the list**, yet frames it as opportunity.
Plans to drop learning **invoicing** because AI makes his weak spot irrelevant.
Guilt about **Agnes**, the receptionist, shows he knows who loses when he wins.

steps.text: Ask the partners for an official systems role and title
Take an evening IT support course for a qualification
Join the office staff union as a lone member

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say we need emergency rules, slow it down, tax the companies, and fund a basic income now. I'd go to the demonstrations. It's the kind of thing I'd actually march about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think every job I could do with my head is gone in two years, including the systems job I'd be so proud of. If AI can do any thinking work, it can run its own setup. So my head start is worth about nothing by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hands-on, fast. My cousin's an electrician and he's been on at me for years to do the apprenticeship, so I'd apply for the spring intake. That buys me the three years before robots, and electricians wire up the robots too. Lena's job is hands-on, so we'd lean on her wage while I'm on apprentice pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, alarmed. AGI by 2028 is the first picture where being good with AI doesn't save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Apprentice pay is low. What gets cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car goes first, I'd sell it and cycle. Then the gym, the takeaways, the trip to see my parents in the summer would be a train, not a flight. We'd burn through the four months of savings in the first year, probably, and Lena would be carrying us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would that sit with you, Lena carrying you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hate it for about a week and then get over it. She carried me before, when I was out of work for two months after school. We're a team, it just feels bad when the team is mostly her.

say: I'd call for **emergency rules**, company taxes and a **basic income** now.
I'd join **demonstrations**, the kind of thing he'd actually march about.
think: Every **head job** I could do is gone by 2028, including the systems role.
My **AI head start** is worth about nothing once AI runs its own setup.
do: Apply for my cousin's **electrician apprenticeship**, spring intake.
Sell the **car**, cycle, and swap flights for trains.
Lean on **Lena's wage** while on apprentice pay.
feel: **Alarmed**, because being good with AI **no longer saves** him.
S2.quote: AGI by 2028 is the first picture where being good with AI doesn't save me.
fieldNote: Sharp turn: the **tech-savvy** junior sees his advantage vanish overnight.
He uses the **three-year robot gap** deliberately, choosing a trade that installs robots.
Household leans on his partner, a **nurse**, whose hands-on work lasts longer.

steps.text: Apply for the spring electrician apprenticeship through his cousin
Sell the car and cycle to work
Live on Lena's nursing wage while on apprentice pay
March at demonstrations for a basic income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so the government should be paying for apprenticeships right now, not after. I'd write to our local representative, which I've never done in my life. At work I'd tell everyone to start thinking about what they'd do with their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to qualify. I'd be thirty-two, a fully trained electrician, with a couple of years before the robots catch up. That's not forever, but it's a proper footing, and I'd still know my way round AI better than most sparkies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the practice for one more year, running the systems and saving hard, aiming for six months of savings. Then I'd start the apprenticeship in 2028, so I qualify around 2031 right as AGI lands. Meanwhile I'd keep using AI every day, because it'll help with quoting and planning jobs as an electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but organised. Like the night before an exam you've actually revised for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the robots in 2034? Doesn't that just move the problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, it does. I'm not going to pretend wiring is safe forever. But I'd rather face the robots at thirty-five with a trade and savings than at twenty-nine with a job that's already gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd write to your representative. What would the letter say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd say: pay people to retrain before they lose their jobs, not after. Fund apprenticeship wages properly so someone with rent can afford to do one. And make the companies that profit pay for it, because they will profit.

say: I'd say government should **fund apprenticeships** now, during the five years.
I'd tell coworkers to plan what they'd do **with their hands**.
think: Five years lets me **qualify** as an electrician by thirty-two.
Knowing **AI** would still give me an edge with quoting and planning jobs.
do: Stay one more year at the practice and save toward **six months**.
Start the **electrician apprenticeship** in 2028, qualifying around 2031.
Write to my **local representative** about funded retraining.
feel: **Anxious** but **organised**, like a well-revised exam night.
S3.quote: I'd rather face the robots at thirty-five with a trade and savings than at twenty-nine with a job that's already gone.
fieldNote: He times his apprenticeship to **qualify** just as thinking AI arrives.
He's honest that the **robot wave** only delays the problem for a trade.
First-ever **political letter** shows how much this would move him.

steps.text: Save toward six months of expenses during one more year at the practice
Write to the local representative about funded apprenticeships
Use AI tools to quote and plan electrical jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, if we start now. Unions should be negotiating retraining deals today. I'd keep posting that it's about who owns the machines, not whether they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel pretty good about it. Ten years means I can try a couple of things, maybe IT support first, then a trade, without panicking. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, with a skill and some savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the practice to pay for the IT support course this year, as part of the systems role. Then in two or three years I'd decide between staying in tech or going for the electrician apprenticeship. Lena and I would also look at buying a small flat, because with ten years of steady work we could actually get a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy at the edges, but mostly excited. There's room to breathe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A mortgage, with AGI coming in 2036? That's a big bet.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and maybe it's stupid. But renting means rent goes up forever, and a mortgage would be nearly half paid by 2036. If it all goes wrong, I'd rather owe a bank for a flat I live in than have nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger version of yourself starting in admin now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the tools, but don't fall in love with the desk. The desk isn't yours. Get something in your hands as well.

Online I'd keep arguing it's about **who owns** the machines.

I'd be **thirty-seven** at the arrival, with a skill and savings.

Choose between **tech and electrics** in two or three years.
Look at buying a **small flat** with Lena on a mortgage.
feel: Mostly **excited**, a little **uneasy** at the edges.
S4.quote: Learn the tools, but don't fall in love with the desk. The desk isn't yours. Get something in your hands as well.
fieldNote: With ten years he turns **optimistic** and starts planning a home.

His advice shows he's absorbed the lesson that **desk work** goes first.

steps.text: Ask the practice to fund an IT support course this year
Decide between IT and an electrician apprenticeship by 2029

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it's the only one where my AI skills count for nothing and I'd be on apprentice pay with Lena carrying us. What would help is paid apprenticeships, wages you can actually live on while training, and a basic income behind that.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I'd use AI to help my own replacement along. I've thought about it. I'd still do it, because someone will, and I'd rather understand it than be surprised by it.

headlineQuote: My boss thinks I'm a wizard, which is funny because I left school at eighteen.
portrait: Nikhil is the **junior administrator** at a nine-person architecture practice and uses AI every day.
He's **progressive**, pro-union, and frames AI as a question of who keeps the **saved time**.
He feels calm in mild worlds, but **AGI by 2028** wipes out his tech advantage.
His escape plan is an **electrician apprenticeship**, timed against the three-year robot gap.
He shares four months of savings with Lena, a **nurse**, whose wage would carry them.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his AI skills count for nothing and money gets tight.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** with livable wages, backed by a **basic income**.
